summary: This work demonstrates temporal-mode engineering for microwave photons using superconducting qubits, generating four orthogonal temporal modes via photon-shaping techniques with fixed-frequency transmons. Mode-selective absorption is achieved with efficiencies exceeding $0.89$ for matched modes and below $0.13$ for orthogonal modes, preserving orthogonality among rejected photons for multiplexed quantum networks.
motivation: Distributed quantum computing requires scalable quantum channels between remote superconducting qubits; leveraging auxiliary degrees of freedom of propagating microwave photons can increase information capacity and enable multiplexing while mitigating photon loss.
method: Single microwave photons in four orthogonal temporal modes are generated by controlling the decay rate $\Gamma_m(t)$ via time-dependent sender drives $\zeta_m^S(t)$ in a resonator-assisted Raman process; selective absorption is implemented by applying the time-reversed receiver drive $\zeta_n^R(-t+\Delta t)$ with independently configurable mode index $n$, and mode orthogonality is verified via squared-overlap matrices $|I_{mm'}|^2$.
result: Process tomography yields averaged fidelity $\mathcal{F} = 0.62$ across four modes for matched-mode quantum state transfer; off-diagonal absorption efficiencies remain suppressed ($R_{m\neq n} \leq 0.13$), and rejected photons preserve mutual orthogonality ($|I_{mm'}|^2 \leq 0.01$ for $m < n$), with simulations indicating potential for fidelity exceeding $0.96$ for matched modes and below $0.01$ for orthogonal modes with improved drive stability.
